subject: Svenska
title: Literary concepts
sourceSummary: Genres, narrative perspective, setting and theme, and figurative language — the core concepts you need to analyse a work of fiction.

questions.prompt: A book about spaceships, time travel and advanced technology in the future belongs to which genre?
questions.opener: Which genre is built on science and technology that don't (yet) exist?
questions.explanation: Science fiction is built on science and technology, often set in the future. Fantasy, by contrast, is about magic and invented worlds without a scientific basis.

questions.opener: What kind of puzzle drives the plot forward?
choices: The plot revolves around solving a crime or mystery
The plot always takes place in a fantasy world
The book has no clear plot
The book is always about love
questions.explanation: Crime fiction (detective novels) revolves around a crime that needs to be solved, often with a detective or police officer as the main character and clues that the reader follows.

questions.prompt: "I didn't know what to say. My hands were shaking as I opened the door." What narrative perspective is this?
questions.opener: Which pronoun tells the story — and whose thoughts do we get access to?
questions.explanation: "I" tells the story and we only get access to that person's own thoughts and feelings — this is a first-person perspective.

questions.prompt: A narrator who knows what ALL the characters in the book are thinking and feeling, even simultaneously in different places, is called:
questions.opener: Which type of narrator has access to everyone's thoughts, not just one person's?
questions.explanation: An omniscient narrator (a third-person perspective with insight into several characters' thoughts) can jump between different characters' inner thoughts and locations.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a story's setting and its theme?
questions.opener: One is WHERE/WHEN the plot happens, the other is what the book is really ABOUT on a deeper level.
choices: There is no difference, the words mean the same thing
Setting is the place and time the plot takes place in, theme is the deeper idea or question the book deals with
Setting is the main character's personality, theme is the plot
The theme is always the title of the book
questions.explanation: Setting = where and when (e.g. a small town in the 1950s). Theme = the overarching idea or question the text explores (e.g. friendship, loneliness, power).

questions.prompt: "Her eyes were like stars." What figure of speech is used here?
questions.opener: Are two things compared using the word "like", or are they equated directly with no comparison word?
questions.explanation: A simile compares two things using words like "like" or "as". A metaphor would have said "her eyes were stars" — without the comparison word, as a direct equation.

questions.prompt: Identify the figure of speech in each sentence and explain which type it is: (1) "The wind whispered through the trees." (2) "He is a lion on the pitch." (3) "Life is a rollercoaster."
questions.opener: Ask of each sentence: is something given human qualities (personification), or are two different things equated completely (metaphor)?
questions.answer: (1) Personification — the wind is given a human ability (to whisper). (2) Metaphor — he is directly equated with a lion (without "like"). (3) Metaphor — life is directly equated with a rollercoaster.
steps: Sentence 1: "the wind whispered" gives the wind a human action (whispering) — this is personification, giving non-human things human qualities.
Sentence 2: "he IS a lion", not "he is LIKE a lion" — the direct equation without a comparison word makes it a metaphor.
Sentence 3: the same pattern as sentence 2 — "life IS a rollercoaster" is a metaphor, not a simile.
Memory tip: a simile contains "like"/"as", a metaphor equates things directly with no comparison word, personification gives things/animals human qualities.

questions.prompt: What are the most common types of figurative language and how do you recognise them?
questions.opener: Four common types to be able to tell apart.
questions.answer: Simile: compares two things using "like" or "as" ("strong as a bear"). Metaphor: equates two things directly with no comparison word ("he is a bear"). Personification: gives non-human things human qualities ("the sun smiled"). Alliteration: several words in a row start with the same letter/sound ("wild winds whisper"). Symbol: a concrete object that stands for something abstract (a dove as a symbol of peace).
